questions.prompt: Pull request A renames `prices.total()` to `prices.sum_prices()` and updates every caller. Pull request B adds a new module that calls `prices.total()`. Both are green on their branches, Git merges both without a conflict, and main fails. What went wrong?
choices: Git's merge algorithm is wrong for Python files
CI was flaky the first time it ran
Each CI run tested its branch against the old main, never the combination that main became; only checks on main + A + B can catch this
B should have been rebased with `--update-refs`
questions.explanation: This is a semantic conflict: the two changes merge cleanly as text and break together. A three-way merge compares lines and cannot see it; only running the checks on the combined tree can, which is exactly what a merge queue does before it moves main.

questions.prompt: CODEOWNERS has `/app/billing/ @acme/payments` on line 6 and `*.sql @acme/dba` on line 7. With code owner review required, whose approval does a change to `app/billing/migrations/0042_refunds.sql` need?
choices: Both teams, because both lines match
@acme/payments, because its pattern is more specific
Nobody, because two lines conflict and GitHub ignores both
Only @acme/dba, because the last matching line decides; move the `*.sql` line above the billing line or add `/app/billing/**/*.sql @acme/payments @acme/dba` after it
questions.explanation: CODEOWNERS is evaluated top to bottom and the last matching line wins, however specific the earlier one is. A later broad pattern silently takes ownership away, which is how the billing migration in The Problem merged without payments.

questions.prompt: A queue with concurrency 3 holds A, B and C. Candidates main+A, main+A+B and main+A+B+C are tested at once: the first and third pass, the second fails. What does the queue do?
choices: Lands A, ejects B, and rebuilds C on main + A to test it again, because C's passing result included B
Lands A and C, ejects B
Lands all three, because the last candidate passed
Ejects all three and starts over
questions.explanation: Results are read in order. A's candidate passed, so A lands. B's candidate failed while everything ahead passed, so B is the cause and is ejected. C's candidate contained B, so its result says nothing about main + A + C; it is rebuilt and tested again.

questions.prompt: Line 16 of CODEOWNERS is `/tools/* @acme/tooling` and line 2 is `* @acme/maintainers`. Who owns `tools/lint.sh` and `tools/ci/run.sh`, and what would the same pattern do in `.gitignore`?
choices: @acme/tooling owns both; `.gitignore` ignores both

@acme/tooling owns `tools/lint.sh` and @acme/maintainers owns `tools/ci/run.sh`, because `dir/*` covers only direct children in CODEOWNERS; in `.gitignore` it ignores both, because an ignored directory hides everything below it
@acme/maintainers owns both, because line 2 matches every file
Neither has an owner, because `*` patterns are not allowed in CODEOWNERS
questions.explanation: GitHub documents that `docs/*` matches `docs/getting-started.md` but not `docs/build-app/troubleshooting.md`. In `.gitignore` the same pattern matches the directory `tools/ci`, and Git never looks inside an excluded directory, so every file below it is ignored.

questions.prompt: Thirty developers each open a pull request every four working hours, CI takes 20 minutes, and the queue tests one candidate at a time. What happens over a week?
choices: Each pull request waits about 20 minutes
The queue keeps up, because short branches rarely fail
Nothing changes compared with long-lived branches
The queue receives 7.5 entries per hour and can finish 3, so its load is 2.5 and the wait grows every hour; test 3 or more candidates at once or batch entries
questions.explanation: Load is arrivals times service time divided by capacity: 30 / 4 entries per hour times one third of an hour, divided by 1 candidate, is 2.5. Above 1 a queue grows without bound. The simulator shows the same team waiting about 20 minutes with four candidates at once.

questions.prompt: A repository enables the GitHub merge queue with `test` as a required check. The workflow that defines `test` has only `on: pull_request`. What happens to queued pull requests?
choices: They merge after their pull request checks, which already passed
GitHub reruns the `pull_request` workflow on the queue branch
Nothing reports `test` for the `gh-readonly-queue/...` branch, so each entry waits until the check timeout and is removed from the queue; add `merge_group` to the workflow's triggers
The queue is disabled until the workflow is fixed
questions.explanation: The queue tests its own candidate branch and fires the `merge_group` event for it. A workflow without that trigger never runs there, the required check stays expected, and `check_response_timeout_minutes` ejects the entry.
